title: Blood Cell Histology, Origin, and Maturation
subject: Hematologic System (HEME)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter teaches how to recognize each blood cell on a stained smear, where those cells come from, and how each lineage matures in the marrow. It then applies that knowledge to the findings boards use most: a high reticulocyte count, a left shift, extramedullary hematopoiesis with splenomegaly, platelet granule defects, and the location of B and T cells in lymph node and spleen. If you can explain what each stain color means and what each maturation step adds or removes, most morphology and lineage questions become reasoning rather than recall.
prerequisites: Basic cell structure: nucleus, ribosomes, mitochondria, granules, and lysosomes
Acid and base properties of dyes and of cell components (DNA, RNA, basic proteins)
Cell cycle and the difference between DNA replication and cell division
Overview of innate and adaptive immune cells and their roles
Oxygen delivery and the stimulus for erythropoietin release from the kidney

connections.how: Normal counts and the function of each cell in this chapter are the reference against which every abnormal blood count is judged.
Heme and globin synthesis happen during the erythroblast stages described here, so defects in either change how precursors mature.
Marrow failure, myelofibrosis, and ineffective erythropoiesis are disorders of the lineages and sites described in this chapter.

terms.def: A marrow cell that can both renew itself and give rise to every blood cell lineage.
A cell descended from the stem cell that has lost self-renewal and is committed to one or a few lineages.
Blood cell production outside the bone marrow, usually in the liver and spleen.
Death of erythroid precursors inside the marrow before they mature, so marrow activity is high but red cell output is low.
A newly released, anucleate red cell that still contains residual ribosomal RNA for about one day in the circulation.

An increase of bands and earlier neutrophil precursors in the blood, reflecting accelerated marrow release.
A blood smear with both nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes, indicating marrow infiltration, fibrosis, or extreme stress.
Repeated DNA replication without cell division, which makes the megakaryocyte large and polyploid.
A lysosome-like neutrophil granule containing myeloperoxidase that is made at the promyelocyte stage.
The cuff of T cells around central arterioles in the splenic white pulp.
A postcapillary venule with cuboidal endothelium in the lymph node paracortex through which lymphocytes enter from blood.

sections.title: Identifying blood cells on a Wright-stained smear

blocks.text: Wright stain is a Romanowsky stain that combines eosin, an acidic dye, with methylene blue and its oxidized azure derivatives, which are basic dyes. Acidic dyes bind basic (positively charged) proteins and stain them orange-pink; this is called eosinophilia. Basic dyes bind acidic material such as DNA, RNA, and sulfated proteoglycans and stain it blue to purple; this is called basophilia. Every color on the smear therefore tells you about chemistry: hemoglobin-filled red cells are pink, nuclei are purple, and cytoplasm rich in ribosomes is blue.

Three features identify almost every cell: size compared with a red cell (about 7 to 8 µm), nuclear shape, and granule color. Use the red cell as a built-in ruler. A small lymphocyte has a nucleus roughly the size of a red cell, a monocyte is about two to two and a half red cells across, and a platelet is a fraction of one.

3 to 5 lobes joined by thin strands
Fine pale pink to lilac granules
Curved, horseshoe shape, no thin strands
Large, uniform, bright orange-red granules that do not hide the nucleus
Coarse dark blue-purple granules over the nucleus

blocks.caption: Normal adult white count is about 4,500 to 11,000/µL and platelet count about 150,000 to 400,000/µL. Percentages are approximate and vary slightly by laboratory.

blocks.text: The granule colors follow from their contents. Eosinophil granules contain major basic protein, a strongly cationic protein in a crystalloid core, so they take up eosin. Basophil granules contain heparin and histamine; heparin is a sulfated, strongly acidic molecule, so the granules bind the basic dyes and turn dark purple. Neutrophil specific granules are close to neutral and stain only faintly, which is why the neutrophil cytoplasm looks pale lilac.

The most common errors involve similar pairs. Lymphocytes and monocytes are both mononuclear, but the lymphocyte is small with a round dense nucleus and a thin rim of cytoplasm, while the monocyte is large with a folded nucleus and gray cytoplasm. A band has a curved but continuous nucleus without the thin strands that join segments, while the earlier metamyelocyte has only a shallow kidney-shaped indent. Large granular lymphocytes (natural killer cells and cytotoxic T cells) carry a few azurophilic granules and should not be mistaken for monocytes. Finally, a platelet lying on top of a red cell can mimic an inclusion; it sits in a different focal plane, while a true inclusion lies within the cell.

sections.title: Hematopoiesis from stem cell to mature lineages

blocks.text: All blood cells descend from the hematopoietic stem cell, a rare marrow cell identified in humans by the surface marker CD34. Its defining properties are self-renewal, so the pool lasts for life, and multipotency, so it can produce every lineage. Most stem cells are quiescent at any moment. When one divides, its daughters either remain stem cells or begin to differentiate into progenitors, which proliferate rapidly but have lost self-renewal and become committed to fewer and fewer lineages.

The first major branch point produces two progenitors. The common myeloid progenitor gives rise to a megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor (red cells and platelets) and a granulocyte-monocyte progenitor (neutrophils and monocytes), and also to eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells. The common lymphoid progenitor gives rise to B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. Monocytes and mast cells finish maturing in tissues, and T cell precursors leave the marrow to complete development in the thymus.

blocks.title: Lineages and the signals that drive them
cols: Key growth factor and its source
rows: Erythropoietin, from peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex
Thrombopoietin, made mainly by the liver
IL-3; stem cell factor for mast cells
IL-7 (lymphoid precursors, especially T cells), IL-15 (NK cells)
blocks.caption: Early-acting factors such as stem cell factor, IL-3, and GM-CSF support several lineages; late-acting factors such as erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, and G-CSF act mainly on one.

blocks.text: Commitment is controlled from inside the cell by lineage-specific transcription factors, which switch on one lineage program and suppress the alternatives. GATA-1, for example, drives erythroid and megakaryocyte genes, while PU.1 drives myeloid and lymphoid genes. Once a cell expresses the receptor for a late-acting growth factor, that factor controls its survival, proliferation, and maturation, so circulating hormones adjust output of each lineage separately according to demand.

The level at which a disease starts determines which cells it affects. Injury to the stem cell itself, as in aplastic anemia, lowers all three myeloid outputs and causes pancytopenia. A mutation in a myeloid stem or early progenitor cell, as in the myeloproliferative neoplasms, can raise red cells, granulocytes, and platelets together. In chronic myeloid leukemia the BCR-ABL fusion arises in a pluripotent stem cell, which is why the Philadelphia chromosome can be found in several lineages and why blast crisis may be myeloid or lymphoid. Loss of one lineage-specific signal, such as low erythropoietin in chronic kidney disease, affects only that lineage.

sections.title: Sites of hematopoiesis and extramedullary hematopoiesis

blocks.text: Hematopoiesis needs a niche: stromal cells, extracellular matrix, and local growth factors that hold stem cells and let them divide. The location of that niche changes during development. Blood islands in the extraembryonic mesoderm of the yolk sac produce the first, mostly erythroid, cells from about week 3. Definitive stem cells, which arise within the embryo itself, then colonize the liver, which becomes the main site of blood formation from about the second month, with a smaller contribution from the spleen. As bones develop marrow cavities, stem cells settle there, and the marrow becomes the dominant site in the last trimester and the only normal site after birth.

blocks.title: Approximate timeline of hematopoietic sites
rows: Primitive, mainly nucleated erythroid cells with embryonic hemoglobins
About week 6 to birth; dominant mid-gestation
Main fetal site; makes fetal hemoglobin (HbF)
Begins mid-gestation; dominant from the last trimester
At birth nearly all marrow is red (active)
Vertebrae, sternum, ribs, pelvis, skull, proximal femur and humerus
blocks.caption: Sites overlap in time; textbooks give slightly different week ranges. In childhood, active marrow in the distal limb bones is gradually replaced by fatty yellow marrow.

blocks.text: The liver and spleen keep the ability to support blood formation after birth. When the marrow is replaced or cannot meet demand, circulating stem cells settle there again and produce blood cells, a process called extramedullary hematopoiesis. The result is hepatosplenomegaly, sometimes with paraspinal masses of hematopoietic tissue.

In primary myelofibrosis, a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm, abnormal megakaryocytes release fibrogenic factors such as PDGF and TGF-beta that stimulate non-clonal fibroblasts to lay down collagen. The scarred marrow cannot hold hematopoiesis, so it moves to the spleen, which may become massive. Red cells forced out through distorted marrow and released from extramedullary sites appear as teardrop cells (dacrocytes), and the poorly regulated release puts nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes into the blood, a leukoerythroblastic smear.

Beta thalassemia major shows the other route to the same outcome. The marrow is not scarred; it is overworked but ineffective, because precursors die before they mature. Symptoms appear at about 6 to 9 months of age, when the switch from gamma to beta globin removes the protection of HbF.

blocks.title: Beta thalassemia major: from globin imbalance to splenomegaly
steps: Beta globin synthesis is absent or severely reduced
Unpaired alpha chains precipitate inside erythroid precursors
Precursors die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis)
Anemia and tissue hypoxia raise erythropoietin
Marrow expands: crew-cut skull, frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth
Liver and spleen resume hematopoiesis
Spleen also enlarges from clearing damaged red cells
blocks.caption: Splenomegaly in beta thalassemia major has two causes: extramedullary hematopoiesis and work hypertrophy from removing abnormal red cells.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with myelofibrosis have a leukoerythroblastic smear, while a patient with iron deficiency anemia of the same severity does not?
blocks.explain: In myelofibrosis, hematopoiesis takes place in fibrotic marrow and in the spleen and liver, which lack the normal marrow-blood barrier and release controls, so nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes escape into the blood. In iron deficiency the marrow architecture is normal and only hemoglobin synthesis is limited, so release stays orderly.
blocks.check: The myelofibrosis paragraph and the definition of extramedullary hematopoiesis.

sections.title: Erythroid maturation and the reticulocyte count

blocks.text: Erythroid maturation has one goal: to fill a small, flexible cell with hemoglobin and then remove everything else. It takes about 5 to 7 days in the marrow. The proerythroblast is large, with open chromatin, nucleoli, and deep blue cytoplasm full of ribosomes ready to make globin. With each division the cell gets smaller, the chromatin condenses, and hemoglobin accumulates while ribosomes decline, so the cytoplasm passes from blue through gray to pink.

blocks.title: Erythroid maturation stages
rows: Nucleus is extruded and engulfed by a marrow macrophage
Faint blue-gray; slightly larger than a mature cell
Keeps ribosomal RNA and some mitochondria; about 1 to 2 days in marrow, about 1 day in blood
No organelles; glycolysis only; lifespan about 120 days
blocks.caption: Hemoglobin accumulates while RNA and nucleus are lost, so cytoplasm turns from blue to pink.

blocks.text: Developing erythroblasts cluster around a central macrophage (an erythroblastic island) that supplies iron and engulfs the extruded nuclei. Because the reticulocyte still has ribosomes and mitochondria, it continues to make a little hemoglobin; the mature cell has neither, so it cannot make protein and depends on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP. The spleen removes any residual nuclear fragments, which is why Howell-Jolly bodies appear after splenectomy.

On Wright stain, reticulocytes appear as slightly large, blue-gray cells (polychromasia). A supravital stain such as new methylene blue, applied to living cells, precipitates the RNA into a dark network, which gives the reticulocyte its name and allows it to be counted. Because each reticulocyte stays in the blood about one day, the count is a direct readout of how many red cells the marrow released recently. The normal reticulocyte count is about 0.5 to 1.5% of red cells.

blocks.title: Erythropoietin feedback loop
steps: Low oxygen delivery to the kidney (anemia, hypoxemia)
HIF stabilizes in renal peritubular interstitial cells
Erythropoietin secretion rises
Erythroid progenitors survive, divide, and mature faster
Reticulocyte count rises after about 3 to 5 days
Hemoglobin and oxygen delivery recover, lowering erythropoietin
blocks.caption: Erythropoietin acts mainly by preventing apoptosis of committed erythroid progenitors, so output rises within days.

blocks.text: With anemia, a high reticulocyte count means the marrow is healthy and answering the loss, which points to hemolysis or bleeding. A low count with anemia means underproduction: iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency, marrow failure or infiltration, or low erythropoietin in kidney disease. The raw percentage must be corrected because anemia lowers the number of mature cells in the denominator, and because erythropoietin releases reticulocytes early, so each one stays in the blood and is counted for longer than one day.

blocks.title: Correcting the reticulocyte count
blocks.text: A patient has a hematocrit of 25% and a reticulocyte count of 9%. First, correct for anemia: 9% x (25 / 45) = 5%. Second, correct for early release using the maturation time in blood, about 1 day at a hematocrit of 45%, 1.5 at 35%, 2 at 25%, and 2.5 at 15%. At 25% the factor is 2, so the reticulocyte production index (RPI) is 5 / 2 = 2.5. An RPI above about 2 indicates an adequate marrow response, consistent with hemolysis or blood loss. An RPI below about 2 points to underproduction, even when the raw percentage looks high.

sections.title: Granulocyte maturation and the left shift

blocks.text: Neutrophil maturation takes about two weeks in the marrow and proceeds through six recognizable stages. Two processes define it. First, granules are made in a fixed order, so the granules present date the cell. Second, the nucleus condenses and then indents and segments, so nuclear shape tracks maturity. The cell can divide only through the myelocyte stage; from the metamyelocyte on it only matures, which creates a large marrow storage pool of nondividing metamyelocytes, bands, and segmented neutrophils ready for release.

blocks.title: Neutrophil maturation stages
rows: Azurophilic (primary) granules made: myeloperoxidase, defensins, elastase
Specific (secondary) granules appear: lactoferrin, lysozyme, collagenase
3 to 5 lobes joined by thin strands
blocks.caption: The promyelocyte is the largest cell of the series. Auer rods in a myeloblast are fused azurophilic granules and indicate acute myeloid leukemia, not normal maturation.

blocks.text: Blood neutrophils exist in two pools of roughly equal size: a circulating pool and a marginated pool rolling along venule walls. A white count measures only the circulating pool. Neutrophils remain in the blood only about 6 to 8 hours and then enter tissues, where they live for a day or two.

In acute bacterial infection, IL-1, TNF, and G-CSF accelerate release from the storage pool faster than cells can finish maturing, so bands and sometimes metamyelocytes and myelocytes appear in the blood. This is a left shift, named for the old practice of recording differentials with immature cells in the left-hand columns. It is often accompanied by toxic changes: toxic granulation (prominent azurophilic granules), Dohle bodies (blue patches of rough endoplasmic reticulum), and cytoplasmic vacuoles. Stress, epinephrine, and glucocorticoids raise the neutrophil count differently: they move marginated cells into the circulating pool and slow their exit into tissues, so the count rises within hours without a left shift.

blocks.title: From bacterial infection to a left shift
steps: Bacteria activate tissue macrophages
IL-1 and TNF released; G-CSF production increases
Marrow storage pool released faster
Bands and earlier forms enter the blood
Neutrophilia with left shift and toxic granulation
blocks.caption: A left shift reflects accelerated release, not a different lineage.

blocks.text: Two distinctions are often tested. A very high count with a marked left shift and toxic changes in a person with infection is a leukemoid reaction; chronic myeloid leukemia instead shows a full spectrum of myeloid cells with basophilia and no toxic changes. A right shift, meaning hypersegmented neutrophils with six or more lobes, reflects impaired DNA synthesis in vitamin B12 or folate deficiency and is not a sign of infection.

blocks.title: Reading a left shift from the differential
blocks.text: White count 18,000/µL with 62% segmented neutrophils, 18% bands, 3% metamyelocytes, 12% lymphocytes, and 5% monocytes. The absolute neutrophil count includes segmented cells and bands: (0.62 + 0.18) x 18,000 = 14,400/µL, above the usual upper limit of about 7,500/µL. Bands alone are 0.18 x 18,000 = 3,240/µL, and at 18% of the count they far exceed the usual upper limit of about 5%; metamyelocytes are also present. The marrow is releasing its storage pool early, the pattern of acute bacterial infection. If the same count had less than 5% bands and no metamyelocytes, demargination from stress or glucocorticoids would be more likely.

Platelets are not cells but fragments of megakaryocytes, the largest cells in normal marrow (about 50 to 100 µm). A megakaryocyte replicates its DNA repeatedly without dividing, a process called endomitosis, and reaches a ploidy of 16N or more within a single lobulated nucleus. The extra DNA supports a very large cytoplasm. An internal demarcation membrane system divides the cytoplasm into future platelet territories, and the megakaryocyte, lying next to a marrow sinusoid, pushes long proplatelet extensions through the sinusoid wall. Blood flow then sheds the platelets, and one megakaryocyte releases thousands.

Thrombopoietin, made at a fairly constant rate by the liver, drives megakaryocyte growth and endomitosis. It is cleared by binding to its receptor (c-Mpl) on platelets and megakaryocytes, so when platelet mass falls, less thrombopoietin is removed, its level rises, and production increases. Platelets circulate for about 7 to 10 days, and about one third of the total platelet mass is held in the spleen, so an enlarged spleen lowers the blood platelet count.

Each platelet has a glycocalyx-coated membrane, a marginal bundle of microtubules beneath it that maintains the disc shape, an open canalicular system connected to the surface, a dense tubular system that stores calcium, and central granules. Because platelets lack a nucleus, they cannot make new protein in response to need; their granules are preloaded.

blocks.title: Platelet granules
rows: Von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, fibronectin, factor V, platelet factor 4, PDGF, TGF-beta; P-selectin in the membrane
Adhesion, fibrinogen bridges for aggregation, coagulation, and wound repair
Recruitment of more platelets (ADP), coagulation cofactor (calcium), vasoconstriction (serotonin)
blocks.caption: Alpha granules hold large proteins; dense granules hold small molecules and ions.

blocks.text: After a vessel is injured, platelets adhere through glycoprotein Ib binding von Willebrand factor on exposed collagen and then release their granules. Secreted ADP binds the P2Y12 receptor on nearby platelets, which activates glycoprotein IIb/IIIa so that it binds fibrinogen and links platelets together. Two contents are commonly misplaced. Serotonin is not made by platelets; they take it up from plasma, where it comes mainly from intestinal enterochromaffin cells. Thromboxane A2 is not stored in granules at all; it is synthesized on activation from arachidonic acid by cyclooxygenase 1. Because platelets cannot make new enzyme, irreversible acetylation of that cyclooxygenase by aspirin lasts for the life of the platelet.

blocks.predict: A patient has a normal platelet count and normal von Willebrand factor but bleeds after minor surgery; platelets aggregate poorly to collagen and show a weak second wave of aggregation. Which granule type is most likely missing, and why?
blocks.explain: Dense granules. Without stored ADP, activated platelets cannot amplify their own signal and recruit neighbors, so the secondary wave that depends on released ADP is blunted. Missing alpha granules would instead give large gray-looking platelets on the smear.

sections.title: B and T cell zones in lymph node and spleen

blocks.text: Secondary lymphoid organs bring together antigen, antigen-presenting cells, and rare lymphocytes that can recognize it. Each organ samples a different fluid: the lymph node filters lymph, and the spleen filters blood. Chemokines keep B and T cells in separate zones. T cells express CCR7 and are drawn to CCL19 and CCL21 in T zones, while B cells express CXCR5 and are drawn to CXCL13 made by follicular dendritic cells.
Lymph node

Afferent lymphatics enter the convex surface and empty into the subcapsular sinus, then cortical sinuses, then medullary sinuses, and leave through the efferent lymphatic at the hilum. The outer cortex contains follicles of B cells. Primary follicles hold naive B cells on a network of follicular dendritic cells; after antigen exposure they become secondary follicles with a pale germinal center, where B cells proliferate and undergo selection, surrounded by a mantle zone. The paracortex (deep cortex) holds T cells, mostly CD4, together with dendritic cells that have carried antigen from tissues. Naive lymphocytes enter the node from blood through high endothelial venules in the paracortex. The medulla contains medullary cords, rich in plasma cells and macrophages, separated by medullary sinuses.

blocks.title: From antigen in lymph to antibody in the medulla
steps: Dendritic cells carry antigen through afferent lymph
Antigen presented to T cells in the paracortex
Activated helper T cells meet B cells at the follicle edge
Germinal center forms in a secondary follicle
Plasma cells settle in medullary cords and secrete antibody
blocks.caption: The layout of the node follows the sequence of an antibody response.

blocks.text: Spleen

Central arterioles branching from trabecular arteries are wrapped by the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath, a T cell zone. B cell follicles sit along the sheath and together they form the white pulp. The marginal zone, at the border between white and red pulp, receives blood first; its macrophages and marginal zone B cells trap blood-borne antigens and respond quickly to polysaccharide antigens of encapsulated bacteria. The red pulp consists of splenic cords (of Billroth), rich in macrophages, and venous sinusoids. In the open circulation, blood released into the cords must squeeze through narrow slits between the sinusoid endothelial cells; old, rigid, or antibody-coated red cells cannot pass and are phagocytosed, and inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies are removed (pitting).

rows: Lymph node follicles and germinal centers
X-linked agammaglobulinemia (absent follicles); enlarged in follicular hyperplasia
DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia); expanded in viral infections
Lymph node medullary cords and sinuses
Sinus histiocytosis in nodes draining a tumor
B cells, marginal zone B cells, macrophages
Asplenia: weak defense against encapsulated bacteria
Splenic red pulp cords and sinusoids
Expanded in hemolytic anemias and extramedullary hematopoiesis
blocks.caption: Which zone is depleted tells you whether the defect is in B cells or T cells.

blocks.text: These zones explain clinical findings. Loss of the spleen (surgery or the autosplenectomy of sickle cell disease) removes the marginal zone and cord macrophages, so people are vulnerable to Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis, and their smears show Howell-Jolly bodies and target cells.

integration.text: Embryology and histology explain where blood is made and why the liver and spleen can make it again: they were fetal blood-forming organs and keep a supportive stroma. Biochemistry explains morphology. The blue of a young cell is ribosomal RNA, the pink of a mature red cell is hemoglobin, eosinophil granules are orange because major basic protein is cationic, and basophil granules are purple because heparin is sulfated. Heme and globin synthesis during the erythroblast stages connect this chapter to disorders of hemoglobin, and the dependence of DNA synthesis on vitamin B12 and folate explains hypersegmented neutrophils.

Immunology and pathology build on the same map. A left shift, a leukemoid reaction, and a leukoerythroblastic smear differ in where and why immature cells leave the marrow. Lymph node and spleen zones reveal whether a defect affects B or T cells. Morphology has limits: cell identification from a smear is a pattern judgment, reference ranges vary by laboratory and age, and a definitive lineage or clonality diagnosis needs flow cytometry, cytogenetics, or marrow biopsy.

summary: Wright stain colors reflect chemistry: basic dyes stain DNA, RNA, and heparin blue to purple; eosin stains hemoglobin and major basic protein pink to orange.
Identify white cells by size relative to a red cell, nuclear shape, and granule color; lymphocytes are small with round nuclei, monocytes large with folded nuclei.
The CD34 positive stem cell self-renews and gives common myeloid (red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes) and common lymphoid (B, T, NK) progenitors.
Blood forms in the yolk sac, then liver (with spleen), then bone marrow; liver and spleen resume production when marrow is fibrotic or ineffective.
Myelofibrosis gives massive splenomegaly, teardrop cells, and a leukoerythroblastic smear; beta thalassemia major gives marrow expansion and hepatosplenomegaly from ineffective erythropoiesis.
Erythroid precursors shrink, gain hemoglobin, lose RNA, and extrude the nucleus; the reticulocyte keeps RNA for about one day in blood.
A reticulocyte production index above about 2 in anemia means the marrow is responding (hemolysis or bleeding); below about 2 means underproduction.
Neutrophils gain azurophilic granules at the promyelocyte and specific granules at the myelocyte, the last dividing stage; a left shift is early release of bands and younger cells.
Megakaryocytes undergo endomitosis and shed platelets; alpha granules hold von Willebrand factor and fibrinogen, dense granules hold ADP, calcium, and serotonin.
B cells occupy node follicles and splenic follicles; T cells occupy the node paracortex and splenic PALS; plasma cells gather in medullary cords.

Normal reticulocyte range is given as about 0.5 to 1.5% here; some laboratories use up to about 2 to 2.5%. The RPI cutoff is given as about 2 here; some sources use 3.
Duration of neutrophil maturation (about 10 to 14 days) and of erythroid maturation (about 5 to 7 days) differs slightly between Junqueira, Guyton and Hall, and hematology texts.
White cell differential percentages and the upper limit of normal for the absolute neutrophil count (about 7,500/µL) vary by laboratory.

The classical branching model (common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors) is used here because it matches the competency; newer research describes a more continuous model with some lineage overlap.
